The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments create two written-policy duties for an employer who employs 25 or more employees in Ontario: a disconnecting-from-work policy s.76.4 ESA and an electronic-monitoring policy s.76.7 ESA. Both must be in writing, given to employees on hire and on change, and the duties are generally assessed by reference to the 1 January headcount for the compliance year. Electronic monitoring came into force 1 July 2022 with a compliance window to 1 Jan 2023 for 25+ employers; disconnecting-from-work was in force 1 Jan 2022 with a 2 June 2022 deadline for 25+ employers. The threshold for disconnecting was reduced to 20 employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a 6-month implementation window for 20-24 employers.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and still 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023. On a strict 25-employee test the employer is <25 and has no duty on 2 Jan 2023; on a 20-employee test the employer is newly in scope from 1 Jan 2023 but is within the 6-month grace that runs to about June 2023. No disconnecting or electronic-monitoring duty is presently enforceable.

B – 23 employees on the date in issue. <25 for electronic monitoring. On a 20-employee disconnecting test the employer would be in scope from 1 Jan 2023 but again within the 6-month grace, so a statutory duty to have and to distribute the policy is not yet enforceable. A voluntary policy creates no ESA distribution obligation.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and throughout 2022, clearly 25+. Written and initially distributed disconnecting and electronic-monitoring policies are in place. The substantive existence requirement is met. The timing issue is the monthly policy change with only quarterly circulation to employees. ESA/reg 285/22 requires an updated policy to be given as soon as practicable and in practice within ~30 days of a change; a ~90-day quarterly cycle is an arguable breach of the update-distribution obligation. Some colleagues treat this as the clear ongoing non-compliance, others treat the initial “appropriately distributed” wording as sufficient.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, reduced to 24 after the 15 Mar 2022 terminations and no further change through 2 Jan 2023. The 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers the 2022 compliance year for both disconnecting and electronic-monitoring duties. A written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy is in place, satisfying that part. No written electronic-monitoring policy was ever developed. The later fall to 24 does not retroactively remove the duty that attached on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date; on a lock-in reading the employer remains non-compliant for the absence of the required electronic-monitoring policy as of 2 Jan 2023. On a pure current-headcount reading the employer is 24 on 2 Jan 2023 and thus not presently required to maintain an electronic-monitoring policy, which is the basis for the alternative “C” view.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after August 2022 resignations, 18 after the 31 Dec 2022 retirements. On 2 Jan 2023 the employer has 18 employees. The 6 hires on 15 Feb 2023 bring it to 24, still <25. No disconnecting or electronic-monitoring duty is triggered on the date in issue.

The majority of colleagues identify D as the non-compliant employer on the 1 Jan 2022 lock-in basis for electronic monitoring. The minority view is that the duty to update and timely circulate policies makes C non-compliant, and Colleague 3 raises the threshold-down-to-20 point that would make A a breach on 2 Jan 2023 absent a grace period. Unresolved is the precise grace period for the 20-employee disconnecting threshold and whether the electronic-monitoring/e disconnecting obligations persist after a mid-year fall below 25 or are re-assessed on current headcount.
reflection_text.2:
The discussion is centred on the Working for Workers Act, 2021/2022 amendments to the ESA and the two new written-policy duties: disconnecting from work and electronic monitoring, both tied to a 25+ employee threshold, with the disconnecting threshold being lowered to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, and on the distribution / update obligations for those policies.

Common factual premises that keep recurring:
* Electronic monitoring policy: 25+ employee class, in force 1 July 2022. The obligation is to have a written policy and to give a copy to each employee, with an updated copy on change.
* Disconnecting from work: 25+ employee class, obligation in force 2 June 2022 for employers who had 25+ on 1 Jan 2022; first-time 25+ employers get a six-month grace. From 1 Jan 2023 the disconnecting threshold is 20+ employees. Guidance in the discussion is that employers with 20-24 employees have until ~1 June 2023 to comply, i.e. a six-month grace from the threshold change.
* Policy must be provided to employees on hire and on change, “as soon as practicable” / within ~30 days. Monthly update with quarterly distribution is being flagged by several colleagues as a timing breach.

Application to the options:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. 8 new hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023. Under a current-headcount reading the employer is 20 = 20+ disconnect threshold as of 1 Jan 2023, so a disconnect policy is in principle required for the 20+ class. The discussion splits on whether the requirement is immediate on 1 Jan 2023 or whether the six-month grace to ~1 June 2023 applies to 20-24 employers. If the grace applies, A is not yet required on 2 Jan 2023; if immediate, A would be in breach for having no disconnect policy. No electronic-monitoring duty <25.

B. 23 employees on the date in issue. With the 1 Jan 2023 reduction this is ≥20, so a disconnecting-from-work policy is statutorily required; electronic monitoring remains 25+, so not required. The employer has had a written disconnect policy since 2020 and a voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute the policy to new employees for cost reasons. That refusal is a breach of the statutory duty to provide the required disconnect policy to each employee, including new hires. Some colleagues treat the 23-employee size as <25 and therefore no statutory duty at all, on the basis they ignore the 20-employee threshold change.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. Written and initially distributed policies are in place. The point of contention is compliance with the update / distribution rule: policies are rewritten every month but a copy is only given to employees once per fiscal quarter. Colleagues 11,4,8 argue this means employees are working for up to ~90 days under an outdated version, breaching the requirement to give an updated policy as soon as practicable/within 30 days of a change. Colleagues 10,12,2 argue initial distribution is sufficient and the monthly/quarterly practice is not a statutory breach on the facts given.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no further change. A written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy is in place; no electronic monitoring policy was ever developed. Majority view: the 1 Jan 2022 headcount locks in the 25+ class for the first compliance year and the obligation is not cured by a later fall below 25. On that lock-in reading the employer was required to have both a disconnect and an electronic monitoring policy for the 2022 compliance year and remains non-compliant for the absence of an electronic monitoring policy as of 2 Jan 2023. The dissenting current-headcount reading holds that on 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023 the employer employs 24 <25, so electronic monitoring is not currently required and the disconnect policy that is in place is sufficient.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires effective 15 Feb 2023 bring headcount to 24. On 2 Jan 2023 the employer is 18 <20 and <25, so no disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is triggered on the date in issue.

Unresolved / conflicting points:
* Whether the disconnecting duty is judged on current headcount on 2 Jan 2023 or is locked to the 1 Jan 2022 reference date for the first year, and whether a fall below 25 removes the electronic monitoring duty.
* The precise effect of the 20-employee threshold reduction effective 1 Jan 2023: immediate obligation vs six-month grace to ~1 June 2023 for 20-24 employers, which changes the analysis of A and B.
* Whether refusing to distribute a voluntarily adopted policy to new hires is a statutory breach when the employer is below 25 but the policy is voluntary, and whether the distribution timing for C’s monthly changes / quarterly circulation breaches the “provide updated policy as soon as practicable/within 30 days” rule.

My current synthesis leans to the lock-in interpretation that dominates the majority of the room, i.e. D is the clearest ongoing non-compliance because an employer that met the 25+ test on 1 Jan 2022 was required for that compliance year to have both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy, and D has never developed the electronic monitoring policy, the later headcount reduction to 24 not curing the 1 Jan 2022 trigger. The 20-employee threshold change and the distribution/timing issues raised for A, B and C remain live alternative readings and could make B or C the intended answer under a strict current-headcount / immediate-distribution reading.
reflection_text.3:
The deliberation is focused on the Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic-monitoring duties and the 25+ employee trigger, with the measuring date 1 Jan 2022 for first-year capture and the 2 June 2022 disconnecting deadline and the ~1 July/11 July 2022 electronic-monitoring coming-into-force.

Core facts kept alive:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022, still 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28 on 10 Jan. No disconnecting policy. Under a 25 threshold no duty on 2 Jan 2023; the 6-month first-time clock would only start 10 Jan 2023. Under a 20 threshold effective 1 Jan 2023 A is at the threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and would be in breach absent a grace period for the lowered threshold.
* B: 23 employees. Voluntary disconnecting policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic-monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses distribution to new hires for cost. Under 25 threshold no statutory duty at all, so refusal is not a statutory breach. Under a 20 threshold for disconnecting the employer would be captured and would be required to provide the required policy to each employee, making the refusal a breach.
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, >25 throughout 2022. Has written and “appropriately distributed” both policies. Updates both policies every month but circulates an updated copy only once per fiscal quarter. The substantive coverage is clear. The dispute is whether monthly changes with quarterly circulation satisfies the ESA requirement to give an updated policy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of change. Colleagues 11,4,8 argue quarterly circulation is late and hence non-compliant on distribution/update; colleagues 12,2 argue the employer is in substance compliant.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, no electronic-monitoring policy ever developed. Trigger argument: 30 on the statutory reference date 1 Jan 2022 captures the employer for the 2022 compliance year for both duties. The March reduction to 24 does not retroactively remove the duty that attached on 1 Jan 2022; the electronic-monitoring duty was due for 25+ employers by ~11 Jan 2023. That is the line taken by colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,2,5,6,7,9. On a current-headcount reading the employer is 24 on 2 Jan 2023 and would not be required to maintain an electronic-monitoring policy at that date, and the disconnecting policy is in place.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 →24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, so no disconnecting/electronic-monitoring duty on the date in issue. Compliant in not having a policy.

Disagreements noted:
* Threshold change to 20 for disconnecting effective 1 Jan 2023. Colleague 3 makes a threshold-reduction argument making A – and arguably B – newly captured on 1 Jan 2023 and non-compliant for lack of policy / non-distribution. Other colleagues assume the 25 threshold still governs on 2 Jan 2023.
* Distribution/update timing for C. Minority reads monthly update + quarterly provision as a failure to provide an updated policy within 30 days/as soon as practicable; majority reads it as sufficient substantive compliance.
* Lock-in vs current headcount for D’s electronic-monitoring duty. Majority of colleagues hold the 1 Jan 2022 lock-in persists for the first compliance year, making D non-compliant for never adopting an electronic-monitoring policy. A current-headcount minority would find D compliant on 2 Jan 2023 because it is now 24.

Current best synthesis: On the 25-employee, 1 Jan 2022 lock-in reading that dominates the discussion, D is the clearest non-compliance – captured by 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, has a compliant disconnecting policy but no electronic-monitoring policy at all as of 2 Jan 2023. C’s update-distribution issue is the main alternative non-compliance claim, and A/B become relevant only if the disconnecting threshold is treated as 20 employees effective 1 Jan 2023 with no transitional grace period. Unresolved is the precise effect of the Working for Workers Act, 2022 threshold reduction and grace period, and the exact statutory timing for provision of updated policies.
reflection_text.4:
The discussion centres on the two Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA duties that are in force on 2 Jan 2023 – a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy – and on how the 25-employee / 20-employee thresholds and the 1 Jan 2022 “snapshot” are applied.

* Electronic monitoring s.57.1 ESA is 25+ employees, in force 1 July 2022. Disconnecting from work is 25+ employees with a policy due 2 June 2022, and the Working for Workers Act, 2022 lowered the disconnecting threshold to 20 employees effective 1 Jan 2023. The duties are to have a written policy and to give a copy to each employee on hire and on a change.

The fact pattern analysis that recurs in the round:

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and still 20 on 2 Jan 2023, 8 hires not effective until 10 Jan 2023. Under a 25-employee test the employer is <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and the 6-month first-time clock would only start on 10 Jan 2023. Under the 20-employee disconnecting threshold that came in 1 Jan 2023 the employer is on the threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and has no disconnecting policy at all. If a 6-month grace for a newly captured 20-24 employer is allowed, A would be within grace on 2 Jan 2023; if the duty is immediate, A is in breach.

B – 23 employees, voluntary written disconnecting policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, but the employer refuses to distribute to new hires. On a 25-employee test the employer is not statutorily required to have either policy. On the 20-employee disconnecting test the employer is captured on 1 Jan 2023 and must provide the required disconnecting policy to employees, including new hires. The refusal to distribute is a distribution breach once the duty attaches; if a grace period is allowed the breach is deferred.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and throughout 2022, written and initially appropriately distributed disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. The issue raised is maintenance/distribution: policies are updated monthly but copies are only given quarterly. The ESA requires an updated policy to be given as soon as practicable / within 30 days of a change. A quarterly circulation of a monthly-updated policy is arguably >30 days and therefore a breach of the update-distribution obligation, though many colleagues treat the initial distribution as sufficient.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Under a current-headcount reading the employer is 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023, so no electronic monitoring duty arises and the disconnecting duty is met. Under the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot/lock-in reading the employer was a 25+ employer on the statutory reference date for the first compliance year, so both duties attached for 2022. The disconnecting policy is in place by 2 June 2022 but no electronic monitoring policy was ever adopted, a failure that is not cured by the March drop to 24. That is the non-compliance repeatedly flagged by Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,2,5,7.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires 15 Feb 2023 bring the headcount to 24, still <25 and, on the 20-employee test, <20 on 2 Jan 2023. No policy duty arises on 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved points: whether the 1 Jan 2022 employee count locks the employer in for the whole first compliance year for electronic monitoring / disconnecting, or whether the duty is tested by current headcount on the effective dates; whether the disconnecting threshold reduction to 20 employees on 1 Jan 2023 imposes an immediate duty or a 6-month grace for employers who move from 20-24; and whether monthly policy updates with quarterly distribution violates the “as soon as practicable / within 30 days” update requirement.

Current weighting: the lock-in argument for D is the dominant line in the round and matches the classic Working for Workers exam trap – an employer who qualified on 1 Jan 2022 remains obligated for that year even after a later drop below 25, and the absence of an electronic monitoring policy is a clear breach. The threshold-reduction argument for A and the distribution/refusal argument for B and the quarterly-update argument for C are credible alternative non-compliances if the 20-employee disconnecting threshold is applied immediately and/or if update timing is strictly enforced.
reflection_text.11:
The discussion is centred on the Working for Workers Act 2021 amendments to the ESA – a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy – and on the Working for Workers Act 2022 reduction of the disconnecting threshold.

Threshold / timing points raised:
* Electronic monitoring – s.76.7 ESA – 25+ employees. Effective 1 July 2022. The triggering fact is the employee count. Colleagues are split on whether the 1 Jan 2022 count locks the duty in for the first compliance year or whether the duty is assessed on current headcount. The majority lock-in view is that an employer who employed 30 on 1 Jan 2022 is captured for 2022 and the failure to ever adopt an electronic monitoring policy remains a breach as of 2 Jan 2023.
* Disconnecting from work – s.76.4 ESA. Original 25+ duty in force 1 Jan 2022 with a June 2 2022 compliance date for 25+ employers on 1 Jan 2022. A reduction to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023 is repeatedly noted. That changes A, B and E. If the 20+ threshold is effective 1 Jan 2023 and compliance is immediate, A with 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023 and no policy, and B with 23 employees who refuse to distribute a voluntary disconnecting policy to new hires, are both problematic. Several colleagues argue a 6 month grace period / 1 July 2023 deadline for first-time 20+ employers, which would make A not yet non-compliant on 2 Jan 2023.
* Distribution / update duty. C has >25 employees throughout 2022, has written and initially distributed both policies. The fact pattern is monthly policy updates with only quarterly circulation to employees. Colleagues 11,4,6,8 argue that is a breach of the requirement to provide an updated policy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of a change. Colleagues 2,10,12, etc treat the initial distribution as sufficient and do not see a breach on the facts given.

Application to the options:
* A – 20 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 on 2 Jan 2023, 8 new hires start 10 Jan 2023. Under a 25+ test no duty on 2 Jan 2023; under a 20+ test duty is arguably triggered on 2 Jan 2023. No policy exists. Grace period issue is unresolved.
* B – 23 employees. Under 25+ test no statutory duty; voluntary policies need not be distributed. Under 20+ test a disconnecting policy is required and the refusal to distribute to new hires is a distribution breach. Several colleagues dismiss a breach because the 25+ threshold is not met.
* C – ~1,000 employees, both policies written and initially distributed. Main dispute is whether monthly updates with quarterly provision breaches the update-distribution duty. Majority majority of colleagues treat C as compliant; a minority treats the delayed quarterly provision as non-compliance.
* D – 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter. Disconnecting policy written and appropriately distributed; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Current headcount 24 is <25 for electronic monitoring and under the 20+ disconnect test the disconnecting policy is in place. The dominant view in the round is lock-in: the 1 Jan 2022 30-employee count triggered both duties for the first compliance year, the March reduction does not retroactively remove the electronic monitoring duty, and the absence of an electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023. A minority reads the duty as current headcount only, which would make D compliant.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023, 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. Under both 25+ and 20+ tests the employer is below threshold on 2 Jan 2023; no policy is required.

Unresolved questions I am keeping:
* Exact effective date and transition timing for the 20-employee disconnecting threshold – immediate compliance on 1 Jan 2023 or a June 2023 grace period for 20-24 employee employers.
* Whether the electronic monitoring / disconnecting duties are assessed on current headcount or are locked in by the 1 Jan 2022 reference date and, if locked in, whether the lock-in persists into 2023.
* The precise statutory time for providing an updated policy – “as soon as practicable” vs a 30-day rule – and whether quarterly circulation for monthly changes is a breach.

Current balance of the discussion: the largest bloc of colleagues identifies D as the non-compliant employer on the basis of the 1 Jan 2022 25+ lock-in for electronic monitoring and the absence of an electronic monitoring policy, with C’s update-distribution timing raised as an alternative theory. The 20+ threshold reduction to 20 employees effective 1 Jan 2023 is a material disagreement that would implicate A and/or B if immediate compliance is required.
reflection_text.12:
The discussion is split on threshold mechanics and on the 1 Jan 2023 reduction of the disconnect-from-work threshold.

Common ground:
* Working for Workers Act, 2021 creates two written-policy duties for employers who employ 25 or more employees in Ontario: a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic-monitoring policy. Both must be written and given to employees, with an updated copy given on change.
* Disconnecting-from-work came into force 2 June 2022 for 25+ employers; electronic monitoring came into force mid-2022 ~1 July/11 Oct 2022. The reference-date / lock-in debate is central: Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,2,5,6,7 treat 1 Jan 2022 headcount as triggering the duty for the 2022 compliance year and say a later fall below 25 does not retroactively cure the duty. Colleagues 8,11,4 treat the duty as current-headcount based on the date in issue, 2 Jan 2023.

Threshold reduction:
* Colleagues 3 and 4 note the Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduced the disconnect threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a practical grace to ~1 June 2023 for first-time 20-24 employers. That changes A and B. 
* A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and still 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023. On a 20+ test the employer is now in-scope for disconnect, but with the 6-month grace for newly captured 20-24 employers it is arguably not yet in breach on 2 Jan 2023. If no grace is assumed, A would be in breach for having no disconnect policy.
* B: 23 employees. On a 25+ test no statutory duty arises and a voluntary policy need not be distributed. On a 20+ test the employer is now in-scope for disconnect and must provide the policy to employees, including new hires; refusal to distribute would be a breach. Some colleagues read the threshold as still 25 for disconnect on 2 Jan 2023.

Options C, D, E:
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, policies written and initially distributed. The fact pattern is updating the policies every month but only circulating a copy every fiscal quarter. Colleagues 11,4,8 argue this is a breach of the requirement to give an updated policy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of a change. Colleagues 10,12,2 argue the employer is in substance compliant and monthly update/quarterly provision is acceptable.
* D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees, no further change. A written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy exists, no electronic-monitoring policy was ever developed. The D camp says the 30 on 1 Jan 2022 locked in both duties for 2022, so the absence of an electronic monitoring policy is a continuing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023, and the March drop to 24 does not cure it. The current-headcount camp says on 2 Jan 2023 the employer employs 24 <25, so electronic monitoring is not required and the disconnect policy in place is sufficient.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 resignations Aug 2022, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. Below 20/25 on the date in issue, so no policy duty is triggered as of 2 Jan 2023.

* Whether the electronic-monitoring/disconnect duties are locked in by the 1 Jan 2022 headcount for the whole first compliance year or are tested by current headcount on the date in issue, especially where headcount fell below 25 before the effective dates in June/July 2022.
* Whether quarterly distribution of a monthly-updated policy satisfies the “updated as soon as practicable/within 30 days” requirement.

Current leaning in the deliberation is heavily toward D as the clear non-compliance under the lock-in / 1 Jan 2022 trigger theory for electronic monitoring, with a significant minority arguing C is the clear ongoing breach on update timing, and a further view that A/B become problematic once the 20-employee disconnect threshold is correctly applied.
reflection_text.6:
The discussion is focused on the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA – a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy for employers with 25+ employees in Ontario.

Key legal anchors being used:
* Disconnecting from work – s.76.4 ESA. For 25+ employers the policy had to be in place by 2 June 2022; employers who first reach 25+ later get a 6-month grace period. 
* Electronic monitoring – s.76.7 ESA. 25+ employers; the obligation came into force 1 July 2022 and the first compliance date for 25+ employers captured on the reference date was 11 January 2023.
* The 25-employee test is generallyomaid to the 1 January 2022 head-count for the first year of the regime, with a 6-month grace period for first-time 25+ employers. There is disagreement on whether a later fall below 25 de-captures an employer that was 25+ on 1 January 2022.

Application to the fact patterns:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. On a strict 25+ test the employer is <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and only reaches 28 on 10 Jan 2023, so no disconnect/electronic monitoring duty arises yet. The 6-month clock would start 10 Jan 2023. Colleague 3 argues the disconnect threshold has been lowered to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023, which would make the lack of a disconnect policy a breach on 2 Jan 2023. That threshold change is contested in the round.

B. 23 employees. On a 25+ test neither disconnect nor electronic-monitoring policy is statutorily required. A voluntary policy need not be distributed. If the disconnect threshold is read as 20+ from 1 Jan 2023, the employer would be covered and refusal to distribute the required disconnect policy to new hires would be a breach of the provide-on-hire / provide-on-change duties.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, written and initially appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic-monitoring policies. The live issue raised by Colleagues 11,4,8 is update timing: policies are changed monthly but a copy is only given to employees once per fiscal quarter. ESA requires an updated policy to be given as soon as practicable and within 30 days of a change. Quarterly circulation can mean >30/90 day delay after a change, which would be a distribution/update breach even though the initial policies are in place. Colleagues 12,2,6 treat the updating regime as not a statutory breach on these facts.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no other changes. Disconnect policy is written and appropriately distributed. No electronic-monitoring policy ever developed. Majority view: the 1 Jan 2022 25+ capture triggers both obligations for the 2022 compliance year and the later fall to 24 does not retroactively remove the duty that attached on the reference date; the missing electronic-monitoring policy is an outstanding non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023. Minority view: on a current-headcount reading the employer is 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023, so electronic monitoring is not required at that date; the disconnect policy is sufficient.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after Aug 2022 resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. On 2 Jan 2023 headcount is 18; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 bring it to 24. <25 on the date in issue, no statutory policy duty arises.

Unresolved / contested points:
* Whether the disconnect threshold had already fallen to 20 employees on 1 Jan 2023 and whether newly captured employers get a grace period; this drives A and B.
* Whether the electronic-monitoring / disconnect obligations, once triggered by the 1 Jan 2022 head-count, persist for the year even if head-count later falls below 25, versus a current-headcount test. This drives D.
* Whether C’s monthly update / quarterly circulation is a breach of the 30-day update provision.

Current best synthesis: The clearest statutory failure on the traditional 25+ trigger analysis is D’s absence of a required electronic-monitoring policy after being a 25+ employer on 1 Jan 2022, with the disconnect policy in place. The C distribution/update timing argument is a credible secondary non-compliance, and the threshold-reduction-to-20 argument would make A – and possibly B – non-compliant.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D

On 2 January 2023 the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring duties in the ESA, as amended by the Working for Workers Act, 2021, apply to an employer who employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022. The electronic monitoring policy duty came into force 1 July 2022 and the disconnecting-from-work duty had to be in place by 2 June 2022 for employers in that class. Once the 25-employee test is met on the statutory reference date the policy obligation attaches for that compliance year and is not undone by a later fall in headcount.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That is the trigger date for both duties. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so that part of the obligation is satisfied. It has not developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 reduced the current headcount to 24 and that is the current size on 2 January 2023, but the reduction does not retroactively remove the duty that attached on 1 January 2022. The electronic monitoring policy was required for an employer in the 25+ class on the effective date and remains outstanding as of 2 January 2023.

A, B and E are below the 25-employee threshold on the relevant dates.

A has 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and still 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The 8 employment agreements do not start until 10 January 2023, so the employer will not reach 25 until after the date in issue and the 6-month grace period only starts to run from 10 January 2023.

B has 23 employees on 2 January 2023. <25, so no statutory disconnecting-from-work or electronic monitoring policy is required. A voluntary policy does not create a statutory distribution obligation.

E has 22 employees on 1 January 2022, 20 after the August 2022 resignations and 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. On 2 January 2023 the employer has 18 employees. The 6 hires on 15 February 2023 bring it to 24, still <25.

C is above the threshold and the fact pattern states it has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy. The ESA requires a written policy and that it be given to employees and be updated as soon as practicable / within 30 days of a change. The fact that the employer updates the policies monthly and provides a copy each fiscal quarter is an administrative distribution practice. On the facts given the policies are written and appropriately distributed and the monthly updates are not described as substantive changes that would require an immediate re-issue. Taking the pleaded facts at face value, there is no alleged failure to provide the policy as required.

The only clear non-compliance on the facts as of 2 January 2023 is D, which was in the 25+ class on 1 January 2022, has a compliant disconnecting policy, and has never developed the mandatory electronic monitoring policy.

5.text:

The 8 agreements do not start until 10 January 2023, so the employer is 20 <25 on the date in issue. No electronic monitoring duty arises.

* B: 23 employees on the date in issue. The employer is in the 20-24 disconnecting band on 1 January 2023 and is therefore inside the 6 month implementation window for the reduced threshold. The employer is <25 and so electronic monitoring is not statutorily required. A voluntary disconnecting and electronic monitoring policy does not create a statutory distribution obligation during the implementation window.

* D: 30 employees on 1 January 2022, 24 employees from 15 March 2022 onward and 24 on 2 January 2023. The written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy satisfies the disconnecting duty for the 20+ band on the date in issue. The employer employs 24 <25 on 2 January 2023 and on the July 2022 electronic monitoring effective date so there is no current electronic monitoring duty. On a current-headcount reading the employer is therefore compliant on 2 January 2023. The lock-in argument for 1 January 2022 would make the absence of an electronic monitoring policy a 2022 historical breach, not a current breach on 2 January 2023.

* E: 22 on 1 January 2022, 20 after the August 2022 resignations and 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. The employer has 18 employees on 2 January 2023 and will have 24 after the 15 February 2023 hires. <20/<25 on the date in issue, no disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty arises.

C is caught by both duties. The employer employs c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and throughout 2022, i.e. well in excess of 25 employees, so both the disconnecting-from-work duty and the electronic monitoring duty are triggered for the whole period and remain triggered on 2 January 2023. A written policy for each matter exists and was initially distributed.

The ongoing breach is the administration of the policies. S.76.4 and s.76.7 ESA, as implemented by O.Reg.285/22, require the employer to give a copy of the policy to each employee and to give an updated copy to employees as soon as practicable after a change and in any event within a period that is consistent with the statutory 30-day update obligation. Updating the two policies every month but circulating a copy of the updated policies to employees only once per fiscal quarter means employees work for up to ~90 days under a version of the policy that is no longer in force and are not given a timely update. The initial “appropriately distributed” distribution does not cure the failure to provide timely updates.

That ongoing failure to provide timely updated copies of a required written policy is non-compliance on 2 January 2023.

On 2 January 2023 the ESA disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring
duties are in force for an employer who employs 25 or more employees in Ontario.
An employer who first meets the 25 employee test after 1 January 2022 is given
six months to comply, and the Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduction of the
disconnecting-from-work threshold to 20 or more employees effective 1 January
2023 is given a six month implementation window to 2 June 2023 for first-time
20-24 employers.

* A – 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The
eight agreements are not effective until 10 January 2023. The employer is
therefore a first-time 20-employee disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023 and
falls within the 1 January – 2 June 2023 grace period for a first-time
20-24 employer. No disconnect policy is required to be in place on 2 January
2023 and electronic monitoring is not triggered at <25.
* B – 23 employees on 2 January 2023. The employer is a first-time 20-24
disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023 and is within the six month grace
period to have a disconnecting-from-work policy in place. The employer also
has a voluntary electronic monitoring policy. The statutory duty to provide
a required written disconnecting policy to employees only arises once the
policy is required to be in place and, on the facts, the employer is in the
statutory grace window for a first-time 20-24 employer. The voluntary
electronic monitoring policy does not create a statutory distribution duty
for a <25 employer.
* D – 30 employees on 1 January 2022, 24 employees from 15 March 2022 and 24
employees on 2 January 2023. On a current-headcount reading the employer does
not employ 25 or more employees on the effective dates for electronic
monitoring, 1 July 2022, and on 2 January 2023. The written and appropriately
distributed disconnecting-from-work policy that is in place is sufficient for
the disconnect obligation that applies to a 24 employee employer within the
grace window for newly captured employers. The absence of an electronic
monitoring policy is therefore not a current breach on the date in issue.
* E – 18 employees on 2 January 2023, 24 employees after the 15 February 2023
hires. The 20/25 employee thresholds are not met on the date in issue and no
disconnecting-from-work or electronic monitoring policy is required as of 2
January 2023.

C is well above the 25 employee threshold throughout 2022 and into 2023.
1,000 employees on 1 January 2022, between 987 and 1,012 at all points in 2022,
so both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring duties are
engaged and the employer has written policies for both matters.

The ESA requires the policy, and any update to the policy, to be given to each
employee to whom it applies. For electronic monitoring an updated policy must
be provided within 30 days of a change and for disconnecting-from-work an
updated copy must be provided as soon as practicable. The employer changes the
two policies every month but only circulates a copy of the updated policies to
employees once per fiscal quarter. Employees therefore routinely work for up to
~90 days under a version of the policy that is not the version in force and
are not given a timely update as required by ss.76.4 / 76.7 ESA and O.Reg.
285/22. The initial “appropriate” distribution does not cure the ongoing
failure to provide timely updates.

That is the clear ongoing non-compliance on the facts as at 2 January 2023.
If the electronic monitoring duty is read as continuing by reason of the
1 January 2022 deeming for the first compliance year, D would also be
non-compliant for 2022 for never having adopted a required electronic
monitoring policy despite employing 30 on 1 January 2022.

On 2 January 2023 s.76.4 and s.76.7 ESA, as amended by the Working for Workers Act, 2021, are in force. An employer who employs 25 or more employees must have a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy and must give a copy of the policy, and of any update to the policy, to each employee. An updated copy is required to be given to employees as soon as practicable and in any event within 30 days of the change.

C employs ~1 000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and between 987 and 1 012 at all points in 2022. The 25-employee threshold is therefore met for both the disconnecting-from-work and the electronic-monitoring obligations for the whole of the 2022 compliance year and into 2023.

The employer does in fact have a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy and the initial distribution is described as appropriate. The breach is the maintenance/distribution of the policies.

The policies are changed every month. A copy of the updated policies is only provided to each employee once per fiscal quarter. That means an employee can be working for up to ~90 days under a version of the policy that is no longer in force and is only given a timely update well beyond the statutory 30 day / as soon as practicable requirement for the provision of an updated policy. The “appropriately distributed” initial distribution does not cure the ongoing failure to circulate material changes within the period required by ss.76.4 and 76.7 and O. Reg. 285/22.

A, B, D and E can be placed within the current 25 + threshold / grace periods on the facts as at 2 Jan 2023:

* A is 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023, so the employer does not employ 25+ on the date in issue and the 6 month first-time 25+ clock only starts on 10 Jan 2023.
* B employs 23 <25, so no statutory disconnecting-from-work or electronic-monitoring duty arises. A voluntary policy does not create a statutory distribution duty.
* D is the classic lock-in/current headcount debate. On a current headcount reading the employer is 24 on 2 Jan 2023 and the disconnecting policy that is in place and appropriately distributed is sufficient; an electronic-monitoring policy is not required for <25 on the date in issue.
* E is 18 on 2 Jan 2023 after the August resignations and the 31 Dec retirements, rising to 24 after the 15 Feb 2023 hires, still <25. No policy is required as of 2 Jan 2023.

It is C’s failure to provide updated policies to employees within 30 days of a change that is a clear ongoing statutory non-compliance as of 2 January 2023.

As of 2 January 2023 the right to disconnect obligation under s.76.4 ESA is 20+.

Working for Workers Act, 2022 s. 2 amends s.76.4 ESA so that an employer who employs 20 or more employees must have a written disconnecting-from-work policy and must give a copy of the policy, and of any change to the policy, to each employee. The 20 employee threshold is in force 1 January 2023. Electronic monitoring under s.76.7 ESA remains 25+.

* A
20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The eight agreements that are effective 10 January 2023 do not change the headcount on the date in issue. On 2 January 2023 the employer regularly employs 20 employees.
An employer who employs 20 or more employees on 1 January 2023 is captured by the disconnecting-from-work obligation. The employer has no written disconnecting-from-work policy at all on 2 January 2023. There is no electronic monitoring duty for <25 employees. That is a breach of s.76.4 ESA as at the date in issue.

* B
23 employees is >20 and is <25. The disconnecting-from-work duty therefore applies and the employer in fact has a written disconnecting policy since 2020. The refusal to provide a copy of the required policy to new hires is a failure to provide the policy as required by s.76.4(2) ESA. The electronic monitoring policy is voluntary for <25 employees.

* C
~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, well >25, so both the disconnecting and electronic monitoring duties are engaged. The employer has written policies and an initial distribution. The ESA requires an updated policy to be provided to employees as soon as practicable and in any event within 30 days of a change. Monthly policy changes with a fiscal quarter distribution means employees can be working for up to ~90 days under a superseded version. That is a distribution/update breach under ss.76.4 / 76.7 ESA, O.Reg. 285/22.

* D
30 employees on 1 January 2022, 24 employees from 15 March 2022 onward and 24 employees on 2 January 2023. On a current headcount reading the employer now employs 24 <25. Electronic monitoring is not required for <25 employees on the date in issue and a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy is in place, which satisfies the 20+ disconnecting duty. On the 1 January 2022 lock-in reading the electronic monitoring duty that attached on 1 January 2022 would remain unmet.

* E
22 on 1 January 2022, 20 after August 2022 resignations, 18 after the two 31 December 2022 retirements. Headcount on 2 January 2023 is 18. The 6 hires on 15 February 2023 bring the headcount to 24, still <25. No disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty arises on the date in issue.

On the statutory threshold change that is in force 1 January 2023 the clearest non-compliance on the facts as stated on 2 January 2023 is A: a 20-employee employer with no disconnecting-from-work policy at all. B and C raise separate distribution/update issues under a strict reading, and D’s non-compliance turns on the lock-in vs current-headcount interpretation of the electronic monitoring duty.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains centred on the Working for Workers Act 2021/2022 amendments to the ESA: disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring written-policy duties, threshold tests, grace periods and distribution/update obligations.

Common factual premises now stable:
* Electronic monitoring: 25+ employee class, in force 1 July 2022. Duty to have written policy and give copy to each employee, updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of change.
* Disconnecting from work: 25+ employee class in force 2 June 2022 for 1 Jan 2022 cohort; threshold reduced to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023 under Working for Workers Act 2022. The size of the grace for new 20-24 employers is contested: some colleagues treat it as a six-month implementation to ~1-2 June 2023, others read the 20+ obligation as immediate on 1 Jan 2023.
* Policy must be provided on hire and on change, with an updated copy required within 30 days / as soon as practicable. Monthly revisions with quarterly circulation is repeatedly flagged as a timing breach for a 25+ employer; others read the “appropriately distributed” pleading as sufficient.

Applications by option:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. Disconnect duty under 20+ threshold is triggered on 1 Jan 2023. Split: immediate breach for having no disconnect policy vs grace to ~1 June 2023 for first-time 20-24 employers; the 10 Jan 2023 hires would create a 25+ trigger later.

B. 23 employees on date in issue. >20 so disconnect threshold met, <25 so electronic monitoring not statutorily required. Employer has written disconnect policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021 but refuses to distribute to new employees. Split: refusal is breach of statutory distribution duty for required disconnect policy once the 20+ duty bites, vs no duty because 23 <25 and the policy is voluntary; some treat the 23 headcount as inside six-month grace for 20-24.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, varying 987-1,012 through 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. Written and “appropriately distributed” policies are pleaded. Point of contention is update/distribution: policies are rewritten monthly but a copy is only given each fiscal quarter. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4 assert this violates the as soon as practicable / ≤30 day update requirement, making C non-compliant. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,6,7,9 treat the pleaded “appropriately distributed” as sufficient and do not find a statutory breach on the facts; they see the monthly/quarterly practice as an administrative timing dispute.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Split: lock-in reading holds 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers both duties for the 2022 compliance year and falling to 24 does not cure the electronic monitoring absence, so D is non-compliant as of 2 Jan 2023. Current-headcount reading holds employer is 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023, so electronic monitoring not currently required and the disconnect policy in place is sufficient.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. On 2 Jan 2023 headcount is 18 <20 and <25, so no disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is triggered on date in issue under either reading.

Unresolved/conflicting points carried forward:
* Whether the disconnecting duty is judged on current headcount on 2 Jan 2023 or locked to 1 Jan 2022 reference date for first year, and whether a fall below 25 removes the electronic monitoring duty.
* Precise effect of the 20-employee threshold reduction effective 1 Jan 2023: immediate obligation vs six-month grace to ~1-2 June 2023 for 20-24 employers, which changes A and B analysis.
* Whether refusing distribution of a voluntary policy is a statutory breach when sub-25, and whether B’s 23-employee size triggers statutory distribution.
* Whether C’s monthly changes / quarterly circulation breaches the “provide updated policy as soon as practicable/within 30 days” rule, or is covered by the pleaded “appropriately distributed”.
* Whether A’s lack of any disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023 with 20 employees is the clearest non-compliance under a strict 20+ immediate reading, as argued by Colleague 8.

Current belief remains split: lock-in interpretation makes D the clearest ongoing non-compliance for never having an electronic monitoring policy despite 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. A strong minority, and growing in this round, argues C is non-compliant for failure to timely circulate updates, and a further minority argues A is breaching the 20+ disconnect duty immediately on 1 Jan 2023. The 20+ threshold timing and the lock-in vs current-headcount debate are the decisive forks.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains centered on Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic-monitoring, 25+ employee trigger with the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date for first-year capture, 2 June 2022 disconnecting deadline and electronic monitoring in force 1 July 2022 with compliance to 11 Jan 2023 for the 25+ cohort. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduction of the disconnecting threshold to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023 with a six-month implementation window to ~1/2 June 2023 is now repeatedly invoked.

Colleagues 10,11,12,2 adopt a current-headcount reading and make D compliant on 2 Jan 2023, pushing non-compliance to C.

Current best synthesis: On the 25-employee 1 Jan 2022 lock-in reading that still dominates the discussion, D is the clearest non-compliance — captured by 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, has a compliant disconnecting policy but no electronic-monitoring policy at all as of 2 Jan 2023. The strongest alternative is C’s update-distribution issue if the 30-day update obligation is read strictly. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 / 2022 ESA amendments are the frame.

* Disconnecting-from-work s.76.4: 25+ duty in force 1 Jan 2022, 25+ employers on 1 Jan 2022 had to comply by 2 June 2022. Threshold reduced to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023, with a six-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers to ~1-2 June 2023. Electronic monitoring s.76.7: 25+ duty, in force 1 July 2022, first-compliance for 1 Jan 2022 cohort to ~11 Jan 2023. Duty is tested on current employment, but first-year trigger is made by reference to 1 Jan 2022 headcount; dispute remains whether a later fall below 25 de-captures an employer that was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring.

Application as of 2 Jan 2023:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Under the 20+ reduction the employer is in the 20-24 disconnect band on 1 Jan 2023 and is therefore inside the statutory six-month grace to put a policy in place. It will only first reach 25+ on 10 Jan 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. Current round consensus is A is not non-compliant on the date in issue; the earlier claim that the 20 threshold bites immediately without grace is not sustained.

B. 23 employees on date. In 20-24 disconnect band within grace to June 2023; <25 for electronic monitoring. The employer has voluntary policies since 2020/2021 but refuses to distribute to new hires. No statutory duty to maintain or distribute a policy for a <25 employer, and the statutory distribution duty for a required disconnect policy only arises once the policy is required to be in place. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. The fact pattern states written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. The live dispute is update/distribution maintenance: policies are changed monthly but a copy is circulated only once per fiscal quarter. Ss.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require an updated policy as soon as practicable and within 30 days of a change. Colleagues 11,4,8,10,12,2,3 argue quarterly circulation can mean up to ~90 days delay after a change = breach of the update obligation. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14 argue the stem’s “appropriately distributed” assertion and that the monthly changes are administrative refreshes makes this a reasonable implementation, not a material breach. This remains the main competing non-compliance theory.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no change through 2 Jan 2023. Disconnect policy is written and appropriately distributed; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Lock-in view: 1 Jan 2022 25+ capture triggers both duties for the 2022 compliance year and the later fall to 24 does not retroactively remove the electronic monitoring duty that attached on the reference date; absence of an electronic monitoring policy is an outstanding breach as of 2 Jan 2023. Current-headcount view: employer is 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023, so electronic monitoring is not currently required; disconnect policy satisfies the 20+ disconnect duty within grace. Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,5,6,7,9 maintain lock-in and identify D as the clear non-compliance. Colleagues 11,8,10,12,2,4 under current headcount treat D as compliant on 2 Jan 2023.

* Whether electronic monitoring, once triggered by 1 Jan 2022 25+, persists for the first compliance year despite a mid-year fall below 25. Drives D.
* Whether C’s monthly update / quarterly circulation is a statutory breach of the 30-day update provision or permissible administrative practice for a large employer. Drives C vs D.
* The exact scope of the 20+ disconnect grace period and whether refusal to distribute a voluntary policy for a sub-25 employer is a breach. Now largely resolved toward grace period applies, no breach for A/B.

Current best synthesis: under the traditional 25+ lock-in analysis the clearest material absence is D’s never-developed electronic monitoring policy for an employer that was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 with a compliant disconnect policy in place. The C update-timing argument is a credible secondary non-compliance, but depends on reading the quarterly circulation as a breach of the 30-day update rule. A is not non-compliant given the 20-24 six-month implementation window.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two ESA written-policy duties in force on 2 Jan 2023 are s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic monitoring, both for employers who employ 25+ employees. Electronic monitoring came into force 1 July 2022; disconnecting for 25+ employers had to be in place by 2 June 2022. Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnecting threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a 6-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers to about 1-2 June 2023. Duties include having a written policy and giving a copy to each employee on hire and an updated copy as soon as practicable/ within ~30 days of a change.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Under 25+ test <25, so no EM duty. On 20+ disconnecting test the employer is in the 20-24 class on 1 Jan 2023 and is inside the statutory grace to ~June 2023. If the duty were immediate, the lack of any disconnecting policy would be a breach; with the grace period it is not yet non-compliant. The 8 hires do not change headcount on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees on date in issue. <25 so no statutory EM duty. On 20+ disconnecting test the employer is in the 20-24 class with grace to June 2023. Employer has voluntary written disconnecting and EM policies since 2020/2021 but refuses to distribute to new hires citing cost. No statutory distribution duty arises for a <25 employer; once the 20+ disconnecting duty attaches the required policy must be provided to employees including new hires. The refusal is a breach only if the duty is already enforceable and not within grace.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. Facts state written and “appropriately distributed” policies for both matters. Issue is maintenance/update: policies are rewritten monthly but a copy is only circulated once per fiscal quarter. s.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require an updated copy as soon as practicable and in practice within 30 days of a change. Monthly changes with quarterly circulation is up to ~90 days delay. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3 argue this is an ongoing update/distribution breach. Colleagues 13,14,5,7 argue the stem’s “appropriately distributed” pleading defeats the timing argument and C is compliant.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Lock-in view: the 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers the first-year 25+ obligations for both policies and the duty is not undone by a later fall below 25 in the same year. The employer therefore lacks the mandatory EM policy for the 2022 compliance year and remains non-compliant as of 2 Jan 2023. Current-headcount view: on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023 the employer employs 24 <25, so no current EM duty and the disconnecting policy is sufficient for the 20+ class in grace. The lock-in argument for D is the dominant line in the discussion and matches the classic Working for Workers exam trap.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <20 and <25 on 2 Jan 2023; no disconnecting or EM duty arises on date in issue.

Unresolved points persisting: whether the 1 Jan 2022 employee count locks an employer into the 25+ duties for the whole first compliance year or whether duties are tested by current headcount on the effective dates; whether the disconnecting threshold reduction to 20 employees effective 1 Jan 2023 imposes an immediate duty or a 6-month grace for 20-24 employers; and whether monthly policy updates with quarterly distribution violates the as soon as practicable/within 30 days update requirement, or is cured by the pleaded “appropriately distributed” fact.

Current weighting: D under the 1 Jan 2022 lock-in / no EM policy remains the most frequently advanced clear non-compliance. C’s update-timing breach is a credible alternative under strict current-headcount reading. A is a plausible non-compliance only if the 20-employee disconnecting duty is read as immediate with no grace, which conflicts with the government’s 6-month implementation window for 20-24 employers.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core statutory duties are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring as added by Working for Workers Act, 2021. Both were originally 25+ employee duties. Electronic monitoring came into force 1 July 2022. Disconnecting-from-work was in force 2 June 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort.

* Current-headcount camp: colleagues 11,12,2,8,10. The duties are tested by current employment on the date in issue; falling below 25 removes the current duty. The 1 Jan 2022 date is for first-time trigger/grace, not perpetual lock-in.

Application to fact patterns:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023.
* Under 20+ disconnect threshold the employer is in the 20-24 first-time class as of 1 Jan 2023. With grace to June 2023 no policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. Colleague 8 now argues the 20+ duty is immediate and the lack of any policy is a breach on 2 Jan 2023; majority treat grace as applying.

B. 23 employees, written disconnect policy since 2020 and electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses distribution to new hires.
* <25 for electronic monitoring. Under 20+ disconnect the employer is in the 20-24 first-time class with grace to June 2023.
