reflection_text.2:
The discussion remains centred on the Working for Workers Act 2021/2022 amendments to the ESA: disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring written-policy duties, threshold tests, grace periods and distribution/update obligations.

Common factual premises now stable:
* Electronic monitoring: 25+ employee class, in force 1 July 2022. Duty to have written policy and give copy to each employee, updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of change.
* Disconnecting from work: 25+ employee class in force 2 June 2022 for 1 Jan 2022 cohort; threshold reduced to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023 under Working for Workers Act 2022. The size of the grace for new 20-24 employers is contested: some colleagues treat it as a six-month implementation to ~1-2 June 2023, others read the 20+ obligation as immediate on 1 Jan 2023.
* Policy must be provided on hire and on change, with an updated copy required within 30 days / as soon as practicable. Monthly revisions with quarterly circulation is repeatedly flagged as a timing breach for a 25+ employer; others read the “appropriately distributed” pleading as sufficient.

Applications by option:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. Disconnect duty under 20+ threshold is triggered on 1 Jan 2023. Split: immediate breach for having no disconnect policy vs grace to ~1 June 2023 for first-time 20-24 employers; the 10 Jan 2023 hires would create a 25+ trigger later.

B. 23 employees on date in issue. >20 so disconnect threshold met, <25 so electronic monitoring not statutorily required. Employer has written disconnect policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021 but refuses to distribute to new employees. Split: refusal is breach of statutory distribution duty for required disconnect policy once the 20+ duty bites, vs no duty because 23 <25 and the policy is voluntary; some treat the 23 headcount as inside six-month grace for 20-24.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, varying 987-1,012 through 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. Written and “appropriately distributed” policies are pleaded. Point of contention is update/distribution: policies are rewritten monthly but a copy is only given each fiscal quarter. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4 assert this violates the as soon as practicable / ≤30 day update requirement, making C non-compliant. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,6,7,9 treat the pleaded “appropriately distributed” as sufficient and do not find a statutory breach on the facts; they see the monthly/quarterly practice as an administrative timing dispute.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Split: lock-in reading holds 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers both duties for the 2022 compliance year and falling to 24 does not cure the electronic monitoring absence, so D is non-compliant as of 2 Jan 2023. Current-headcount reading holds employer is 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023, so electronic monitoring not currently required and the disconnect policy in place is sufficient.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. On 2 Jan 2023 headcount is 18 <20 and <25, so no disconnect or electronic monitoring duty is triggered on date in issue under either reading.

Unresolved/conflicting points carried forward:
* Whether the disconnecting duty is judged on current headcount on 2 Jan 2023 or locked to 1 Jan 2022 reference date for first year, and whether a fall below 25 removes the electronic monitoring duty.
* Precise effect of the 20-employee threshold reduction effective 1 Jan 2023: immediate obligation vs six-month grace to ~1-2 June 2023 for 20-24 employers, which changes A and B analysis.
* Whether refusing distribution of a voluntary policy is a statutory breach when sub-25, and whether B’s 23-employee size triggers statutory distribution.
* Whether C’s monthly changes / quarterly circulation breaches the “provide updated policy as soon as practicable/within 30 days” rule, or is covered by the pleaded “appropriately distributed”.
* Whether A’s lack of any disconnect policy on 2 Jan 2023 with 20 employees is the clearest non-compliance under a strict 20+ immediate reading, as argued by Colleague 8.

Current belief remains split: lock-in interpretation makes D the clearest ongoing non-compliance for never having an electronic monitoring policy despite 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. A strong minority, and growing in this round, argues C is non-compliant for failure to timely circulate updates, and a further minority argues A is breaching the 20+ disconnect duty immediately on 1 Jan 2023. The 20+ threshold timing and the lock-in vs current-headcount debate are the decisive forks.
reflection_text.3:
The discussion remains centered on Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic-monitoring, 25+ employee trigger with the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date for first-year capture, 2 June 2022 disconnecting deadline and electronic monitoring in force 1 July 2022 with compliance to 11 Jan 2023 for the 25+ cohort. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduction of the disconnecting threshold to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023 with a six-month implementation window to ~1/2 June 2023 is now repeatedly invoked.

Core facts kept alive:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 on 2 Jan 2023, 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 → 28. No disconnecting policy. Under 25 threshold no duty on 2 Jan 2023; a 6-month first-time clock would start 10 Jan 2023. Under 20 threshold effective 1 Jan 2023 the employer is in the 20-24 band on 2 Jan 2023 with a grace to ~June 2023. Colleague 8 argues A is non-compliant now for having no policy; majority treat A as within grace.
* B: 23 employees. Has voluntary disconnecting policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic-monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses distribution to new hires for cost. Under 25 threshold no statutory duty. Under 20 threshold for disconnecting the employer would be captured and would need to provide the required policy to each employee, making the refusal a distribution breach. Majority in round 1 treat B as sub-threshold and compliant.
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Written and “appropriately distributed” disconnecting and electronic-monitoring policies. Updates policies every month but circulates an updated copy only once per fiscal quarter. Majority of the lock-in camp now argue the monthly change + quarterly circulation breaches the s.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 requirement to provide an updated policy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of change. Colleague 1,5,7,13,14 argue the facts state policies are written and appropriately distributed and the quarterly cadence is acceptable for a large employer.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, no electronic-monitoring policy ever developed. Lock-in camp: 30 on 1 Jan 2022 captures employer for 2022 compliance year for both duties; reduction to 24 does not retroactively remove duty; electronic-monitoring policy required for 25+ cohort by ~11 Jan 2023 remains outstanding → non-compliant. Current-headcount camp: employer is 24 on 2 Jan 2023 and on 1 July 2022, so no electronic-monitoring duty currently applies and the disconnecting policy is sufficient.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 →24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no duty.

Disagreements crystallised in round 1:
* Threshold reduction to 20 for disconnecting effective 1 Jan 2023. Colleague 3 and 8 use it to make A – and arguably B – newly captured on 1 Jan 2023 and non-compliant for lack of policy / non-distribution. Others apply a six-month grace to 1/2 June 2023 and keep A/B within window.
* Distribution/update timing for C. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3 now treat monthly updates with quarterly circulation as a clear breach of the 30-day/as soon as practicable update rule. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14 treat the pleaded “appropriately distributed” as dispositive and see only an administrative timing dispute.
* Lock-in vs current headcount for D’s electronic-monitoring duty. Majority of colleagues 1,13,14,5,6,7,9 maintain 1 Jan 2022 lock-in persists for first compliance year, making D non-compliant for never adopting an electronic-monitoring policy. Colleagues 10,11,12,2 adopt a current-headcount reading and make D compliant on 2 Jan 2023, pushing non-compliance to C.

Current best synthesis: On the 25-employee 1 Jan 2022 lock-in reading that still dominates the discussion, D is the clearest non-compliance — captured by 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, has a compliant disconnecting policy but no electronic-monitoring policy at all as of 2 Jan 2023. The strongest alternative is C’s update-distribution issue if the 30-day update obligation is read strictly. A becomes relevant only if the 20-employee disconnecting threshold is treated as immediately operative on 1 Jan 2023 with no grace period, and B becomes relevant under that same threshold reduction plus a distribution duty. Unresolved are the precise effect of the Working for Workers Act, 2022 threshold reduction and its grace period, the statutory interpretation of “as soon as practicable” for monthly policy refreshes, and whether electronic-monitoring duties attach by lock-in or by current headcount after a mid-year fall below 25.
reflection_text.6:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 / 2022 ESA amendments are the frame.

* Disconnecting-from-work s.76.4: 25+ duty in force 1 Jan 2022, 25+ employers on 1 Jan 2022 had to comply by 2 June 2022. Threshold reduced to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023, with a six-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers to ~1-2 June 2023. Electronic monitoring s.76.7: 25+ duty, in force 1 July 2022, first-compliance for 1 Jan 2022 cohort to ~11 Jan 2023. Duty is tested on current employment, but first-year trigger is made by reference to 1 Jan 2022 headcount; dispute remains whether a later fall below 25 de-captures an employer that was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring.

Application as of 2 Jan 2023:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Under the 20+ reduction the employer is in the 20-24 disconnect band on 1 Jan 2023 and is therefore inside the statutory six-month grace to put a policy in place. It will only first reach 25+ on 10 Jan 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. Current round consensus is A is not non-compliant on the date in issue; the earlier claim that the 20 threshold bites immediately without grace is not sustained.

B. 23 employees on date. In 20-24 disconnect band within grace to June 2023; <25 for electronic monitoring. The employer has voluntary policies since 2020/2021 but refuses to distribute to new hires. No statutory duty to maintain or distribute a policy for a <25 employer, and the statutory distribution duty for a required disconnect policy only arises once the policy is required to be in place. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. The fact pattern states written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. The live dispute is update/distribution maintenance: policies are changed monthly but a copy is circulated only once per fiscal quarter. Ss.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require an updated policy as soon as practicable and within 30 days of a change. Colleagues 11,4,8,10,12,2,3 argue quarterly circulation can mean up to ~90 days delay after a change = breach of the update obligation. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14 argue the stem’s “appropriately distributed” assertion and that the monthly changes are administrative refreshes makes this a reasonable implementation, not a material breach. This remains the main competing non-compliance theory.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no change through 2 Jan 2023. Disconnect policy is written and appropriately distributed; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Lock-in view: 1 Jan 2022 25+ capture triggers both duties for the 2022 compliance year and the later fall to 24 does not retroactively remove the electronic monitoring duty that attached on the reference date; absence of an electronic monitoring policy is an outstanding breach as of 2 Jan 2023. Current-headcount view: employer is 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023, so electronic monitoring is not currently required; disconnect policy satisfies the 20+ disconnect duty within grace. Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,5,6,7,9 maintain lock-in and identify D as the clear non-compliance. Colleagues 11,8,10,12,2,4 under current headcount treat D as compliant on 2 Jan 2023.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 resignations Aug 2022 →20, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 →18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 →24. <20 and <25 on date in issue. No policy duty arises as of 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved/contested:
* Whether electronic monitoring, once triggered by 1 Jan 2022 25+, persists for the first compliance year despite a mid-year fall below 25. Drives D.
* Whether C’s monthly update / quarterly circulation is a statutory breach of the 30-day update provision or permissible administrative practice for a large employer. Drives C vs D.
* The exact scope of the 20+ disconnect grace period and whether refusal to distribute a voluntary policy for a sub-25 employer is a breach. Now largely resolved toward grace period applies, no breach for A/B.

Current best synthesis: under the traditional 25+ lock-in analysis the clearest material absence is D’s never-developed electronic monitoring policy for an employer that was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 with a compliant disconnect policy in place. The C update-timing argument is a credible secondary non-compliance, but depends on reading the quarterly circulation as a breach of the 30-day update rule. A is not non-compliant given the 20-24 six-month implementation window.
reflection_text.4:
The two ESA written-policy duties in force on 2 Jan 2023 are s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic monitoring, both for employers who employ 25+ employees. Electronic monitoring came into force 1 July 2022; disconnecting for 25+ employers had to be in place by 2 June 2022. Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnecting threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a 6-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers to about 1-2 June 2023. Duties include having a written policy and giving a copy to each employee on hire and an updated copy as soon as practicable/ within ~30 days of a change.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Under 25+ test <25, so no EM duty. On 20+ disconnecting test the employer is in the 20-24 class on 1 Jan 2023 and is inside the statutory grace to ~June 2023. If the duty were immediate, the lack of any disconnecting policy would be a breach; with the grace period it is not yet non-compliant. The 8 hires do not change headcount on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees on date in issue. <25 so no statutory EM duty. On 20+ disconnecting test the employer is in the 20-24 class with grace to June 2023. Employer has voluntary written disconnecting and EM policies since 2020/2021 but refuses to distribute to new hires citing cost. No statutory distribution duty arises for a <25 employer; once the 20+ disconnecting duty attaches the required policy must be provided to employees including new hires. The refusal is a breach only if the duty is already enforceable and not within grace.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties. Facts state written and “appropriately distributed” policies for both matters. Issue is maintenance/update: policies are rewritten monthly but a copy is only circulated once per fiscal quarter. s.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require an updated copy as soon as practicable and in practice within 30 days of a change. Monthly changes with quarterly circulation is up to ~90 days delay. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3 argue this is an ongoing update/distribution breach. Colleagues 13,14,5,7 argue the stem’s “appropriately distributed” pleading defeats the timing argument and C is compliant.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Lock-in view: the 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers the first-year 25+ obligations for both policies and the duty is not undone by a later fall below 25 in the same year. The employer therefore lacks the mandatory EM policy for the 2022 compliance year and remains non-compliant as of 2 Jan 2023. Current-headcount view: on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023 the employer employs 24 <25, so no current EM duty and the disconnecting policy is sufficient for the 20+ class in grace. The lock-in argument for D is the dominant line in the discussion and matches the classic Working for Workers exam trap.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <20 and <25 on 2 Jan 2023; no disconnecting or EM duty arises on date in issue.

Unresolved points persisting: whether the 1 Jan 2022 employee count locks an employer into the 25+ duties for the whole first compliance year or whether duties are tested by current headcount on the effective dates; whether the disconnecting threshold reduction to 20 employees effective 1 Jan 2023 imposes an immediate duty or a 6-month grace for 20-24 employers; and whether monthly policy updates with quarterly distribution violates the as soon as practicable/within 30 days update requirement, or is cured by the pleaded “appropriately distributed” fact.

Current weighting: D under the 1 Jan 2022 lock-in / no EM policy remains the most frequently advanced clear non-compliance. C’s update-timing breach is a credible alternative under strict current-headcount reading. A is a plausible non-compliance only if the 20-employee disconnecting duty is read as immediate with no grace, which conflicts with the government’s 6-month implementation window for 20-24 employers.
reflection_text.12:
The core statutory duties are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring as added by Working for Workers Act, 2021. Both were originally 25+ employee duties. Electronic monitoring came into force 1 July 2022. Disconnecting-from-work was in force 2 June 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort. 

Threshold reduction: Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduced the disconnecting-from-work threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 January 2023. Colleagues 10,11,12,2 now accept a six-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers to  ~1-2 June 2023. Electronic monitoring remains 25+.

Lock-in vs current headcount remains the central split.

Disconnect trigger debate:
* Lock-in / 1 Jan 2022 reference date camp: colleagues 1,13,14,5,6,7,9,4. Once 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 the disconnect and electronic monitoring duties attach for the 2022 compliance year and are not retroactively cured by a later fall below 25. 
* Current-headcount camp: colleagues 11,12,2,8,10. The duties are tested by current employment on the date in issue; falling below 25 removes the current duty. The 1 Jan 2022 date is for first-time trigger/grace, not perpetual lock-in.

Application to fact patterns:

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023.
* Under 20+ disconnect threshold the employer is in the 20-24 first-time class as of 1 Jan 2023. With grace to June 2023 no policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. Colleague 8 now argues the 20+ duty is immediate and the lack of any policy is a breach on 2 Jan 2023; majority treat grace as applying.

B. 23 employees, written disconnect policy since 2020 and electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses distribution to new hires.
* <25 for electronic monitoring. Under 20+ disconnect the employer is in the 20-24 first-time class with grace to June 2023. Majority says no statutory distribution duty arises yet for the required policy and a voluntary policy need not be distributed. Colleagues 3,8 argue refusal to distribute a required 20+ disconnect policy is a breach; the voluntary nature is disputed.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 through 2022. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Policies updated monthly, copy circulated quarterly.
* Unquestionably 25+ so both duties engaged throughout. The dispute is update timing. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3 argue s.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require an updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of a change; monthly changes with quarterly circulation = up to ~90 day delay = breach. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,6,7,9 argue the fact pattern states “appropriately distributed” and monthly revisions/quarterly circulation is a reasonable administrative cadence for a large employer; no per se breach established.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
* Lock-in camp: 30 on 1 Jan 2022 triggered both duties for 2022; disconnect is satisfied, electronic monitoring never developed = continuing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023; later fall to 24 does not cure.
* Current-headcount camp: on 1 July 2022 effective date and 2 Jan 2023 the employer employs 24 <25, so electronic monitoring is not currently required; disconnect policy is in place and sufficient for 24 employees within the 20+ grace window.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 resignations Aug 2022, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24.
* 18 <20/<25 on 2 Jan 2023. No policy duty arises on date in issue. Consensus.

Unresolved questions:
* Whether the 20+ disconnect reduction is operative immediately on 2 Jan 2023 or subject to a six-month grace for first-time 20-24 employers, and whether that grace excuses A and B.
* Whether the electronic monitoring/disconnect duties are locked in by 1 Jan 2022 headcount for the first compliance year or are tested by current headcount on 2 Jan 2023, especially where headcount fell below 25 before the July 2022 effective date.
* Whether quarterly distribution of a monthly-updated policy satisfies “as soon as practicable / within 30 days” or is a material breach.

Current distribution in round 1: strong D lock-in camp 1,13,14,5,6,7,9,4; C update-breach camp 10,11,12,2,3; A immediate 20+ breach minority 8. reflection_text.8:
The discussion remains about the Working for Workers Act, 2021 / 2022 amendments to the ESA, the 25-employee trigger for electronic monitoring and the 20-employee trigger for disconnecting-from-work effective 1 Jan 2023, and how the trigger is assessed, whether a duty persists after headcount falls, and the update/distribution duties.

Key legal facts repeatedly raised in both rounds:
* Disconnecting from work s.76.4 ESA. 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 → policy by 2 June 2022. Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduced the threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a first-time 20-24 grace window that is commonly read as to ~1-2 June 2023. Policy must be in writing and given to employees; updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of change.
* Electronic monitoring s.76.7 ESA. 25+ employees, in force 1 July 2022. Policy must be in writing and distributed to employees, updates as soon as practicable / within 30 days.
* Test for first year: lock-in on 1 Jan 2022 headcount vs current headcount on date in issue. Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,5,6,7,9 continue to argue the 1 Jan 2022 headcount locks the employer in for the first compliance year and a later fall below 25 does not retroactively remove the duty. Colleagues 11,8,2,4 argue a current-headcount reading for 2 Jan 2023.

Positions on the fact patterns in current round:
* A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. 25+ view: no duty on 2 Jan 2023. 20+ view: employer is in the 20-24 disconnect band as of 1 Jan 2023. Colleague 8 and Colleague 3 argue no disconnect policy at all on 2 Jan 2023 is a breach of s.76.4. Colleagues 10,11,12,1 note a 6-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers to ~June 2023, so A is inside grace and not yet non-compliant. No electronic monitoring duty <25.
* B – 23 employees, written disconnect policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses to distribute to new employees for cost. 25+ view: no statutory duty at all. 20+ view: employer is in 20-24 disconnect band as of 1 Jan 2023, policy exists but refusal to provide it to new hires is a distribution breach under s.76.4(2). Colleagues 1,10,11,12,14,5,7 treat <25 as no duty, so voluntary policy refusal is not a statutory breach. Colleague 3 flags distribution failure once 20+ threshold is applied.
* C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, >25 throughout 2022. Written and initially appropriately distributed both policies. Issue is update timing: policies changed every month, copy circulated only every fiscal quarter. Colleagues 11,12,2,4,8 argue this is up to ~90 days after a change, breaching the as soon as practicable / 30 day update requirement of ss.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7 argue the stem states policies are written and appropriately distributed and quarterly circulation of monthly refreshes is a reasonable administrative practice for a large employer, no per se breach alleged.
* D – 30 employees 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, no further change. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy. Lock-in view: employer was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 so electronic monitoring duty attached for 2022 and remains unmet as of 2 Jan 2023; headcount fall to 24 does not cure it. Current-headcount view: on 2 Jan 2023 employer has 24 <25, so electronic monitoring duty not applicable now; disconnect duty for 24 employees is met by existing policy, with 20+ grace to June 2023. Majority of colleagues in round 1 still select D on lock-in.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 Aug 2022 =20, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 →24. On 2 Jan 2023 headcount 18 <20/25, so no disconnect or electronic monitoring duty arises on date in issue. Universally treated as compliant.

Disagreements and errors noted:
* Whether the disconnecting threshold is 25 on 2 Jan 2023 or has been reduced to 20 effective 1 Jan 2023 and whether a grace period applies. This drives A and B analyses.
* Lock-in vs current headcount for electronic monitoring, driving D. The split is stable across both rounds.
* Whether refusal to distribute a voluntary policy creates liability for a sub-25 employer. Colleagues are split on B.
* Whether quarterly distribution of monthly policy changes satisfies “provide updated policy as soon as practicable / within 30 days”. This drives C.

Current best understanding after round 1:
The 20-employee disconnect threshold effective 1 Jan 2023 is law as of 2 Jan 2023. That makes A a potential non-compliance for having no disconnect policy at all for a 20-employee employer, but it may be saved by the 6-month first-time 20-24 implementation window that many colleagues cite. B becomes problematic on distribution if the 20+ threshold is applied. C has a plausible breach on update timing under a strict reading of the 30-day update rule, and D’s non-compliance hinges on the lock-in interpretation of electronic monitoring. The majority of colleagues in round 1 still favour D on a lock-in 25+ analysis, with a significant minority favouring C on update timing, and a growing minority noting A is the cleanest non-compliance once the 20-employee threshold is taken literally without grace.

* Precise effective date/compliance deadline for electronic monitoring for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort and whether the duty is deemed to continue after a mid-year fall below 25.

reflection_text.11:
The discussion remains centred on the Working for Workers Act 2021 ESA amendments – s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic monitoring – and the Working for Workers Act 2022 reduction of the disconnecting threshold.

Threshold / timing points now repeated:
* Electronic monitoring – 25+ employees, in force 1 July 2022. Duty is to have a written policy and give a copy to employees and an updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of change. Dispute persists on whether the duty is assessed on current headcount or is locked in by the 1 Jan 2022 reference date for the first compliance year. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,6,7,9 maintain lock-in: an employer who was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 remains captured for 2022 and the absence of an electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,8 maintain a current-headcount reading: once below 25 the electronic monitoring duty ceases.
* Disconnecting from work – 25+ in force 1 Jan 2022, 2 June 2022 compliance date for 25+ on 1 Jan 2022. Threshold reduced to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023. Dispute on transition: immediate compliance on 1 Jan 2023 vs a 6-month implementation window to ~2 June 2023 for first-time 20-24 employers. The 20+ reduction changes the assessment of A, B and E.
* Distribution / update duty. s.76.4 / s.76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require initial provision, provision to new hires, and provision of an updated policy as soon as practicable and in practice within 30 days of a change. C has ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, written and initially “appropriately distributed” disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies, updates the policies every month but circulates a copy to employees only once per fiscal quarter. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3 argue the monthly change / quarterly circulation is a breach of the timely-update obligation. Colleagues 1,5,7,13,14 treat the fact pleading “written and appropriately distributed” as sufficient and view the timing as an administrative practice, not a statutory breach.

Application to options as of 2 Jan 2023:
* A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → 28. Under 25+ test no duty on 2 Jan 2023. Under 20+ test the employer is in the 20-24 band on 2 Jan 2023. If immediate compliance is required, no disconnecting policy is a breach; if a 6-month grace to ~2 June 2023 applies, no breach yet. Electronic monitoring never triggered <25.
* B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. Under 25+ test no statutory duty. Under 20+ test disconnecting policy is required in the 20-24 band, with or without grace. Employer has written disconnecting policy since 2020 and electronic monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute to new employees citing cost. Under 25+ test no distribution duty; under 20+ test the refusal to provide the required policy to new hires is a distribution breach.
* C – 1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Both policies written and initially appropriately distributed. The main live dispute is the monthly update / quarterly circulation. Majority in this round now treat C as the clearest non-compliance on update-distribution timing; a minority treats C as compliant on the pleaded facts.
* D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Lock-in view: captured on 1 Jan 2022 for both duties, electronic monitoring policy due from 1 July 2022 and remains absent as of 2 Jan 2023 → non-compliant. Current-headcount view: 24 <25 on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023, electronic monitoring not required, disconnecting policy in place → compliant. Disconnecting duty under 20+ test is also satisfied.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023, 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <20 and <25 on 2 Jan 2023. No policy required on the date in issue under either 25+ or 20+ test, even with grace.

Unresolved questions kept:
* Exact effective date and transition timing for the 20-employee disconnecting threshold – immediate compliance 1 Jan 2023 or a six-month grace to June 2023 for 20-24 employers.
* Whether electronic monitoring / disconnecting duties are assessed on current headcount or locked in by the 1 Jan 2022 reference date, and if locked in, whether the lock-in persists into 2023.
* Precise statutory timing for updated policies – “as soon as practicable” vs a 30-day rule – and whether quarterly circulation for monthly changes constitutes non-compliance, especially where the facts state policies were “appropriately distributed”.

Current balance: A sizable bloc now identifies C as non-compliant on timely update/distribution grounds under a current-headcount reading with the 20+ threshold in force. The largest historical bloc still identifies D as non-compliant on the 1 Jan 2022 lock-in for electronic monitoring. A third view identifies A as the clearest breach under an immediate 20+ compliance reading. B remains a borderline distribution issue dependent on the 20+ threshold and grace period.

reflection_text.10:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 duties are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring for an employer who employs 25 or more employees in Ontario. Electronic monitoring came into force 1 July 2022 with first-year compliance to 1 Jan 2023 for 25+ employers; disconnecting-from-work was in force 1 Jan 2022 with 2 June 2022 deadline for 25+ employers. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnecting-from-work threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023 with a six-month implementation window for 20-24 employers, i.e. policy due ~1-2 June 2023. Electronic monitoring remains 25+.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. On a 25+ test the employer is <25 and not yet required. On the new 20+ disconnect test the employer is a first-time 20-24 employer as of 1 Jan 2023 and is inside the six-month grace to ~June 2023. No electronic monitoring duty <25. The 8 hires do not change headcount on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees on date in issue. <25 for electronic monitoring. For disconnecting the employer is in the 20-24 band on 1 Jan 2023 and therefore inside the six-month grace; a written disconnect policy exists since 2020 and a voluntary electronic monitoring policy exists since late 2021. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy to new hires is not a statutory ESA distribution duty while the employer is <25 and within the disconnect grace window.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. 25+ threshold is clearly met for both duties throughout. The fact pattern states written and “appropriately distributed” disconnecting and electronic-monitoring policies exist. The continuing issue is maintenance/update: policies are rewritten every month but an updated copy is only given to employees once per fiscal quarter. S.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require an updated copy to be given as soon as practicable and in practice within ~30 days of a change. Monthly changes with quarterly circulation means employees can work up to ~90 days under a superseded version. A minority of colleagues treat this as the clear ongoing non-compliance; a majority treat the stated “appropriately distributed” initial distribution as sufficient and argue the timing is an administrative matter for a large employer.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations on 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, 24 on 2 Jan 2023. A written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy is in place. No written electronic-monitoring policy was ever developed. Lock-in vs current headcount debate:
* Lock-in reading: the 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers the first compliance year for both duties; falling below 25 mid-year does not retroactively remove the duty that attached on the reference date. Absence of an electronic-monitoring policy for a 1 Jan 2022 25+ employer is an outstanding non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023.
* Current-headcount reading: on 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023 the employer employs 24 <25, so no current electronic-monitoring duty arises, and the existing disconnect policy is sufficient for the 20+ disconnect duty which for a 24-employee employer is within the 20-24 grace to June 2023.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, -2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, -2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24, still <25. No disconnecting or electronic-monitoring duty arises on 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved points: whether the electronic-monitoring duty is tested by current employment or is locked in for the calendar year first triggered on 1 Jan 2022, and whether the monthly-rewrite/quarterly-circulation practice for C is a material breach of the 30-day / as soon as practicable update requirement or can be read as “appropriately distributed” on the facts as pleaded. The 20+ disconnect grace period for A and B is now widely accepted, which removes A as an immediate breach. The central split remains D lock-in missing electronic-monitoring policy vs C timely-update failure.

The Working for Workers Act, 2021/2022 duties in force on 2 Jan 2023 are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring.

* Disconnecting-from-work: 25+ in force 1 Jan 2022, first compliance 2 June 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort. Threshold reduced to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023 by Working for Workers Act, 2022 with a six-month implementation window for first-time 20-24 employers, ~1-2 June 2023.
* Electronic monitoring: 25+ duty, in force 1 July 2022. First-year compliance for the 25+ class to 1 Jan 2023. Debate remains whether the duty for the first compliance year is locked to the 1 Jan 2022 headcount or tested by current employment on the effective date / 2 Jan 2023.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring. First-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 Jan 2023, inside the six-month grace to ~June 2023. Widely accepted as compliant on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees on date in issue. <25 for electronic monitoring. 20-24 disconnect band on 1 Jan 2023, inside six-month grace. Employer has voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021 and refuses distribution to new hires. No statutory distribution duty for a sub-25 employer / during grace; refusal of voluntary policy is not an ESA breach. Accepted as compliant.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023, +6 hires 15 Feb 2023 =24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no disconnect / electronic monitoring duty arises on date in issue. Accepted as compliant.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties throughout and on 2 Jan 2023. Stem expressly pleads written and “appropriately distributed” disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies.

Disagreement is maintenance/update. S.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require initial distribution, distribution to new hires, and an updated copy as soon as practicable after a change, with a ~30-day outer limit for electronic monitoring updates. Fact pattern: policies rewritten every month, updated copy circulated once per fiscal quarter. 

C proponents argue this is an ongoing breach: employees work up to ~90 days under superseded versions, failing the as soon as practicable / ≤30 day update requirement despite initial “appropriately distributed” pleading.

D proponents argue the pleaded fact of “written and appropriately distributed” is dispositive; monthly internal refreshes with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000-person employer is a reasonable practicable process and does not convert a pleaded compliant initial distribution into a per se breach.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 →24 thereafter, 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy in place; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.

Lock-in reading: 1 Jan 2022 headcount met the 25+ class for the first compliance year of both duties. Disconnect duty satisfied. Electronic monitoring duty attached on 1 Jan 2022 reference date, in force 1 July 2022 for that cohort; falling to 24 mid-year does not retroactively remove the duty that attached for the 2022 year. Absence of any electronic monitoring policy is an outstanding non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023.

Current-headcount reading: on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023 employer employs 24 <25, so no current electronic monitoring duty arises; disconnect policy is sufficient for a 24-employee employer within the 20+ grace window.

Round 2 split is D lock-in / missing electronic monitoring policy vs C timely-update failure. Majority of colleagues in round 2 adopt lock-in for D and treat C’s “appropriately distributed” pleading as not establishing a material breach; a minority adopt current-headcount for D and treat C’s monthly-rewrite/quarterly-circulation as a material breach of the update distribution obligation.

Unresolved points that remain material: whether electronic monitoring duty for the first compliance year is locked to the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date or tested by current employment on the effective date; whether the monthly revision / quarterly circulation for C is a material breach of the as soon as practicable / 30-day update requirement or can be read as consistent with “appropriately distributed” as pleaded; and whether the 20+ disconnect grace window is correctly applied to A and B as first-time 20-24 employers.

6.text:
As of 2 January 2023 the duties in issue are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring under the Working for Workers Act, 2021, as implemented by O.Reg.285/22.

First-year attachment is measured by the 1 January 2022 headcount. An employer who is 25+ on that reference date is captured for the first compliance year. The duty that attaches on the reference date is not retroactively unwound by a mid-year fall in headcount during that compliance year.

* Disconnecting-from-work was in force 1 January 2022 for 25+ with a 2 June 2022 compliance date for the 1 January 2022 cohort. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnecting threshold to 20+ effective 1 January 2023 with a six month first-time 20-24 implementation window to ~1-2 June 2023.
* Electronic monitoring is a 25+ duty in force 1 July 2022. The first-year cohort is the employers who were 25+ on 1 January 2022.

Applied to the options:

A. 20 employees on 2 January 2023; the 8 hires do not start until 10 January 2023. First-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023, inside the six month grace. <25, no electronic monitoring duty on the date.

B. 23 employees on the date. <25 for electronic monitoring and in the 20-24 disconnect first-time band within the six month grace to ~June 2023. The existing policies are voluntary. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy to new hires is not a statutory distribution duty for a sub-25 employer within the grace window.

E. 18 employees on 2 January 2023 after the August resignations and the 31 December retirements; 24 after the 15 February 2023 hires. <20/<25 on the date in issue. No disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty arises on 2 January 2023.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Both duties are engaged for the whole period and remain engaged on 2 January 2023. The stem expressly pleads a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy and a written and appropriately distributed electronic monitoring policy. S.76.4/76.7 require provision on adoption, to new hires within a reasonable time, and an updated copy as soon as practicable after a change. The pleaded fact of appropriate distribution, together with the context of monthly internal refreshes with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000 person employer, does not establish the material statutory absence pleaded elsewhere. This is an administrative timing debate, not the clear absence of a required policy.

D. 30 individuals on 1 January 2022, 24 from 15 March 2022 onward and 24 on 2 January 2023. On the statutory reference date D was a 25+ employer for both duties for the 2022 compliance year. D has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so that limb is satisfied.

D has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. Electronic monitoring was required for the 25+ first-year cohort from 1 July 2022. The six terminations on 15 March 2022 reduced current headcount to 24, but that mid-year reduction does not remove the obligation that attached on 1 January 2022 for the compliance year in which the duty attached. The complete absence of a mandatory electronic monitoring policy for an employer captured on the 1 January 2022 measuring date remains outstanding as of 2 January 2023.

That is a material statutory failure on the facts as of 2 January 2023, whereas A, B and E are below threshold or within the statutory 20-24 grace window, and C is pleaded as having the required written and appropriately distributed policies.

D.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: As of 2 January 2023 the in-force duties from the Working for Workers Act, 2021 are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting from work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring. For the first compliance year both duties are triggered by the 1 January 2022 measuring date and once the 25+ class is met on that reference date the policy obligation attaches for that year. A mid-year fall below 25 does not retroactively unwind a duty that attached on the statutory measuring date.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. On that measuring date it is a 25+ employer for both regimes. Disconnecting from work was in force 1 January 2022 with a 2 June 2022 first compliance date for the 1 January 2022 cohort. Electronic monitoring is in force 1 July 2022 for the 25+ class.

D has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so that limb is satisfied. D has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. Headcount fell to 24 on 15 March 2022 after the six terminations and remains 24 on 2 January 2023, but that mid-year reduction does not remove the obligation that attached on 1 January 2022 for the 2022 compliance year. The electronic monitoring policy required for a 25+ employer from 1 July 2022 for the 1 January 2022 cohort is therefore an outstanding statutory absence as of 2 January 2023.

The other options are compliant on the facts as of 2 January 2023.

A is 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The eight agreements are effective and start 10 January 2023. The employer is a first-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023 under the Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduction and is inside the six month implementation window to ~1-2 June 2023. It is <25 so no electronic monitoring duty arises.

B is 23 employees on the date in issue. <25 for electronic monitoring and in the 20-24 disconnect grace window to ~2 June 2023. The employer already has voluntary policies. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy while the employer is sub-threshold and within the implementation window is not a statutory ESA breach.

E is 18 employees on 2 January 2023 after the August resignations and the 31 December retirements. The six hires on 15 February 2023 bring it to 24, still <25. No disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty arises on the date in issue.

C is being over-read on update timing. The stem expressly pleads the employer has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy and employs c.1,000 employees throughout 2022, so both duties are clearly engaged. Ss.76.4 and 76.7 require a written policy, distribution on adoption and to new hires, and an updated copy to be provided as soon as practicable after a change. The pleaded fact is appropriate distribution. Monthly internal refreshes with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000-person employer is a reasonable administrative cadence and is consistent with “as soon as practicable”. The stem does not plead a material substantive change that went uncommunicated, nor does it allege failure to give the initial policy or to give an update within a reasonable time. Characterising routine housekeeping edits as per se statutory changes requiring redistribution within 30 days infers a breach beyond what is pleaded.

On a pleaded-facts reading the only clear material statutory absence is D: a 25+ employer on the 1 January 2022 reference date with a compliant disconnecting policy in place but with no electronic monitoring policy ever developed for the compliance year in which the duty attached.

3.text:

Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnecting threshold to 20+ effective 1 January 2023 with a six month first-time 20-24 implementation window to ~1-2 June 2023.
* Electronic monitoring is a 25+ duty in force 1 July 2022. The first compliance cohort is the employers who were 25+ on the statutory measuring date 1 January 2022. Once the 25+ class is met on that measuring date the policy obligation attaches for the first compliance year and is not retroactively undone by a mid-year fall in headcount during that year.

A is 20 employees on 2 January 2023; the 8 agreements do not start until 10 January 2023. The employer is a first-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023 and is inside the 6 month implementation window to June 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring. No breach on 2 January 2023.

As of 2 January 2023 the two written policy duties in force are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting from work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring, made by the Working for Workers Act, 2021 and O.Reg.285/22.

* Disconnecting from work is 25+ in force 1 January 2022 with a 2 June 2022 first compliance date for the 1 January 2022 cohort. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnecting threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 January 2023. First-time 20-24 employers have a six month implementation window to about 1-2 June 2023.
* Electronic monitoring is a 25+ duty in force 1 July 2022. The duty is tested on current employment.

On a current head-count reading as of 2 January 2023

A – 20 employees on 2 January 2023; the 8 hires do not start until 10 January 2023. The employer is a first-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023 and is therefore inside the six month implementation window to ~ June 2023. <25 so no electronic monitoring duty arises.

B – 23 employees on the date in issue. <25 for electronic monitoring and in the 20-24 first-time disconnect band on 1 January 2023, inside the six month implementation window to ~2 June 2023. The employer has a voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and a voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy to new hires is not a statutory distribution duty for a sub-25 employer during the implementation window.

D – 30 employees on 1 January 2022, 24 employees from 15 March 2022 onward and 24 on 2 January 2023. On 1 July 2022, the electronic monitoring effective date, the employer already employed 24 <25 employees. On a current head-count reading there is no current electronic monitoring duty and a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy is in place, which is sufficient for a 24 employee employer within the 20+ implementation window.

E – 22 on 1 January 2022, 20 after the August 2022 resignations and 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. The employer has 18 employees on 2 January 2023 and will have 24 after the 15 February 2023 hires. <20/<25 on the date in issue, no disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty arises on 2 January 2023.

C is in scope for both duties. The employer employs c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022, well in excess of 25, so both the s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work duty and the s.76.7 electronic monitoring duty are engaged for the whole period and remain engaged on 2 January 2023. A written policy for each matter exists and was initially distributed.

The continuing obligation is maintenance and timely distribution of updates. Ss.76.4 and 76.7 ESA and O.Reg.285/22 require a copy of the policy to be given to each employee on adoption and on hire and an updated copy to be provided as soon as practicable after a change and, for electronic monitoring, in any event within a period consistent with the statutory 30 day update obligation. Updating both policies every month but circulating a copy of the updated policies to employees only once per fiscal quarter means employees routinely work for up to ~90 days under a version of the policy that is no longer in force and are not given a timely update as required. Initial “appropriately distributed” distribution does not cure the ongoing failure to provide timely updated copies.

That ongoing failure to provide updated written policies within the as soon as practicable / ≤30 day window is non-compliance on 2 January 2023.

The electronic monitoring policy required for a 25+ employer from 1 July 2022 is therefore still outstanding as of 2 January 2023. That is a material statutory absence, not a timing dispute.

A is 20 on 2 January 2023; the eight agreements do not start until 10 January 2023. It is a first-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 January 2023 and is inside the six month implementation window to ~2 June 2023. No electronic monitoring duty arises <25.

E is 18 on 2 January 2023 after the August resignations and the 31 December retirements. The six hires on 15 February 2023 only bring it to 24, still <25. No duty arises on 2 January 2023.

C is being over-read on the update timing point. The stem expressly pleads that the employer has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy, and employs c.1,000 employees throughout 2022. That is the statutory requirement. Ss.76.4 and 76.7 require the policy to be given on adoption, to a new employee within a reasonable time, and an updated copy to be given as soon as practicable after a change. “As soon as practicable” is contextual and O.Reg.285/22 does not convert every internal monthly refresh into a per se 30/90 day breach.

Monthly internal edits with a quarterly consolidated circulation to a ~1,000-person employer is a reasonable administrative process for non-material housekeeping changes and is consistent with the pleaded fact of appropriate distribution. There is no pleaded allegation of a material substantive change that was not communicated within a practicable period, nor a failure to give the initial policy. The initial “appropriately distributed” finding is not cured by an inferential dispute about whether a monthly revision must be pushed out within 30 days.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The frame remains Working for Workers Act, 2021 / 2022 amendments to ESA: s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic monitoring, implemented by O.Reg.285/22. Disconnect 25+ in force 1 Jan 2022, first compliance 2 June 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort; threshold reduced to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023 with a six-month first-time 20-24 implementation window to ~1-2 June 2023. Electronic monitoring 25+ in force 1 July 2022; first-year cohort is employers with 25+ on the statutory reference date 1 Jan 2022. Duties require a written policy, initial distribution, distribution to new hires, and an updated copy as soon as practicable / within 30 days of a change.

* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. On 2 Jan 2023 employer is 20 <25, first-time 20-24 disconnect employer within the six-month grace to June 2023. No electronic monitoring duty. Consensus compliant.
* B: 23 employees on date. <25 for electronic monitoring; in 20-24 disconnect grace. Has voluntary policies since 2020/2021 but refuses to distribute to new hires on cost. No statutory duty to maintain/distribute for a sub-25 employer in the grace window. Consensus compliant.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. On 2 Jan 2023 headcount is 18 <20/<25. No disconnect or electronic monitoring duty on date. Consensus compliant.

Disputed pair:

C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Stem pleads “written and appropriately distributed both a policy on disconnecting from work and a policy on electronic monitoring.” Policies are rewritten every month but a copy is circulated to employees only once per fiscal quarter. 
Lock-in/pleaded-facts view, held by Colleagues 1,11,12,13,14,3,4,5,6,7,8,9: “written and appropriately distributed” is the statutory requirement; monthly internal refresh with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000 person org is reasonable practicable administration and “as soon as practicable” is contextual. No pleaded absence of a required policy, only an administrative cadence dispute.
Current-headcount/update-timing view, held by Colleagues 10,2 and in round 0 by Colleague 11: Updating monthly but circulating quarterly means employees work up to ~90 days under an out-of-date version, breaching the as soon as practicable / ≤30 day update obligation for electronic monitoring and for disconnecting. That ongoing failure to provide timely updated copies is non-compliance.

D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, no change through 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
Lock-in view, held by Colleagues 1,11,12,13,14,3,4,5,6,7,8,9: The 1 Jan 2022 headcount triggers both duties for the 2022 compliance year and the duty is not retroactively removed by a mid-year fall below 25. Electronic monitoring was in force from 1 July 2022 for the 25+ first-year cohort. Complete absence of a mandatory electronic monitoring policy for an employer captured on the reference date is a material, clear non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023. Disconnect policy is in place and the 24 headcount is within the 20+ grace window.
Current-headcount view, held by Colleagues 10,2 in this round, and previously by Colleagues 11,12,2,8: Duty is assessed by current regular employment. On 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023 employer employs 24 <25, so no current electronic monitoring duty arises. Disconnect policy satisfies the 20+ duty within the grace window. Under this reading D is compliant on date and the only ongoing breach is C’s update/distribution timing.

Current best synthesis remains the lock-in analysis: D is the clearest material statutory absence – a 25+ employer on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date with a compliant disconnect policy but no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. C’s update-timing theory is a credible secondary non-compliance but depends on reading quarterly circulation as a per se breach of the update rule and is contested by the pleaded “appropriately distributed” language. Colleagues 10 and 2 have shifted in this round to the current-headcount reading for D and to C as the answer; the majority in round 3 still hold D as the primary breach.

Unresolved: whether electronic monitoring, once triggered by 1 Jan 2022 25+, persists for the first compliance year despite a mid-year fall below 25, driving D; and whether C’s monthly update / quarterly circulation is a statutory breach of the 30-day/update-as-soon-as-practicable rule.

The core duties at issue on 2 January 2023 are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring, made by Working for Workers Act, 2021 and implemented in O.Reg.285/22.

* Disconnecting-from-work: 25+ in force 1 Jan 2022, first compliance 2 June 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort. Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces the disconnect threshold to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023. First-time 20-24 employers as of 1 Jan 2023 get a six-month implementation window to ~1-2 June 2023.
* Electronic monitoring: 25+ duty in force 1 July 2022. The first-year class is anchored to the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date for the initial cohort.

Lock-in vs current headcount remains the central split.

* Lock-in / 1 Jan 2022 reference date camp: colleagues 1,11,12,13,14,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Once 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 the disconnect and electronic monitoring duties attach for the 2022 compliance year and are not retroactively cured by a later fall below 25 during that year. The 1 Jan 2022 measurement is the statutory trigger for the first year.
* Current-headcount camp: colleagues 10,2. Duties are tested by current regular employment on the effective date / date in issue; falling below 25 removes current duty. The 1 Jan 2022 date is for first-time trigger/grace, not perpetual lock-in.

Application under the prevailing 20+ grace reading now in round 3:

A. 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. First-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 Jan 2023, inside six-month grace to June 2023. <25, no electronic monitoring. Compliant on 2 Jan 2023.

B. 23 employees. <25 for electronic monitoring. 20-24 disconnect band with six-month grace to June 2023. Voluntary policies since 2020/2021 do not create statutory distribution duty while sub-25 / in grace. Refusal to distribute voluntary policy is not an ESA breach on the date in issue.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug resignations → 18 after 31 Dec retirements. 18 on 2 Jan 2023; hires 15 Feb 2023 bring to 24 <25. No disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty arises on 2 Jan 2023. Consensus compliant.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Both duties engaged. Stem expressly pleads written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring policies.
Dispute is update timing: policies updated monthly, copy circulated quarterly.
C camp 10,2 argue s.76.4/s.76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days; monthly changes with quarterly circulation = up to ~90 day delay = breach.
D camp 1,11,12,13,14,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 argue pleaded fact is “appropriately distributed.” Monthly internal refresh with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000 person employer is reasonable administrative cadence / “as soon as practicable”; no pleaded material substantive change withheld, no failure to give initial policy. Characterising housekeeping edits as per se breach is inferential beyond pleadings.

D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
Lock-in camp: 30 on 1 Jan 2022 triggered both duties for 2022; disconnect satisfied, electronic monitoring never developed = continuing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023; later fall to 24 does not cure.
Current-headcount camp: on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023 employer employs 24 <25, so electronic monitoring not currently required; disconnect policy in place and sufficient for 24 employee within 20+ grace.

Current round distribution is D 12 vs C 2, up from D 9 vs C 5 in previous reflection. Majority now strongly favors D as clearest statutory absence: a 25+ employer on the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date with a compliant disconnect policy but no electronic monitoring policy ever developed for the compliance year in which the duty attached.

Unresolved questions remain:
* Whether electronic monitoring/disconnect duties are locked in by 1 Jan 2022 headcount for first compliance year or tested by current headcount on 2 Jan 2023, especially where headcount fell below 25 before July 2022 effective date.
* Whether quarterly distribution of monthly-updated policy satisfies “as soon as practicable / within 30 days” or is material breach; pleaded “appropriately distributed” fact is read differently.
* Precise effect of Working for Workers Act, 2022 20+ reduction on existing voluntary policies and distribution duties for 20-24 band during six-month grace.

My current understanding aligns with the lock-in majority: D is the only employer with a pleaded material statutory absence – 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 reference date, required electronic monitoring policy never developed – while A, B, E are within thresholds/grace and C is pleaded as having the required written and appropriately distributed policies.

Debate on update cadence: policies changed monthly but copy circulated quarterly. Minority 10,2 hold strict breach: monthly change → up to ~90 day delay vs “as soon as practicable”/30-day update requirement. Majority in round 3 treat pleaded “written and appropriately distributed” as satisfying s.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22; monthly internal refresh with quarterly consolidated circulation for ~1,000-person employer is reasonable practicable administration, not a pleaded material absence.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 →24 thereafter, no further change. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two ESA written-policy duties in force on 2 Jan 2023 are s.76.4 disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 electronic monitoring, both from Working for Workers Act, 2021, implemented by O.Reg.285/22.

Electronic monitoring: 25+ duty in force 1 July 2022. For the first compliance year the 25+ class is fixed by the statutory measuring date 1 Jan 2022. Once 25+ on that reference date the written policy obligation attaches for the 2022 compliance year and is not retroactively unwound by a mid-year fall below 25 during that year. Duties include a written policy, initial distribution on adoption and to new hires, and an updated copy as soon as practicable / within ~30 days of a change.

Threshold / lock-in is the central dispute that has now converged:

A – 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 so no EM duty. First-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 Jan 2023, inside six-month grace to ~June 2023. No breach on 2 Jan 2023.

B – 23 employees on date in issue. <25 for EM. In 20-24 disconnect band with grace to ~June 2023. Policies since 2020/2021 are voluntary while sub-25 / within grace. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a statutory distribution duty on 2 Jan 2023.

The pleaded “appropriately distributed” is taken as meeting the statutory existence/initial distribution requirement. The monthly internal refresh with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000-person employer is now treated by the majority as administrative maintenance consistent with “as soon as practicable”; no pleaded material substantive change withheld or failure to give initial policy. The earlier C-update-timing breach argument is now viewed as inferential beyond pleaded facts.

D – 30 individuals on 1 Jan 2022, fired 6 on 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, 24 on 2 Jan 2023. On the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date D was 25+ for the first compliance year of both s.76.4 and s.76.7. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy is in place, satisfying that limb and also compatible with current 24 headcount in the 20+ disconnect grace.

No written electronic monitoring policy ever developed. EM was required for the 25+ first-year cohort from 1 July 2022 with first compliance to 1 Jan 2023. The mid-year fall to 24 does not remove the obligation that attached on 1 Jan 2022 for the 2022 compliance year. Complete absence of the mandatory EM policy for an employer captured on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date remains an outstanding breach as of 2 Jan 2023.

The Working for Workers Act, 2021/2022 duties in force on 2 Jan 2023 are s.76.4 ESA disconnecting-from-work and s.76.7 ESA electronic monitoring, implemented by O.Reg.285/22.

* Disconnecting-from-work: 25+ in force 1 Jan 2022, first compliance 2 June 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort. Working for Workers Act, 2022 reduces threshold to 20+ effective 1 Jan 2023 with a six-month first-time 20-24 implementation window to ~1-2 June 2023.
* Electronic monitoring: 25+ duty in force 1 July 2022. For the first compliance year the class is fixed by the statutory measuring date 1 Jan 2022. An employer who is 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 is captured for the 2022 compliance year and the policy obligation that attaches on the measuring date is not retroactively undone by a mid-year fall below 25 during that year. First compliance for that cohort is to 1 Jan 2023.

Fact patterns as of 2 Jan 2023:

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring. First-time 20-24 disconnect employer as of 1 Jan 2023, inside six-month grace to ~June 2023. Compliant.

B – 23 employees on date in issue. <25 for electronic monitoring. First-time 20-24 disconnect band on 1 Jan 2023, inside six-month grace. Employer has voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and voluntary electronic monitoring policy since late 2021 and refuses distribution to new hires. No statutory distribution duty for sub-25 / during grace; refusal of voluntary policy not an ESA breach. Compliant.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022 =20, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 =18 on 2 Jan 2023, +6 hires 15 Feb 2023 =24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no disconnect/electronic monitoring duty arises on date in issue. Compliant.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ for both duties throughout and on 2 Jan 2023. Stem expressly pleads written and “appropriately distributed” disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. 
Majority round 4 view: “appropriately distributed” is pleaded as fact; monthly internal refresh with quarterly consolidated circulation for a ~1,000-person employer is reasonable practicable administrative cadence consistent with “as soon as practicable” and the statutory requirement to give initial policy and updates to new hires. No pleaded material substantive change withheld. No material breach found on pleaded facts.
Minority view persists: s.76.4/76.7 and O.Reg.285/22 require updated copy as soon as practicable after change, with ~30 day outer limit for electronic monitoring; monthly rewrites with quarterly circulation = up to ~90 day delay.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, fired 6 employees 15 Mar 2022 →24 thereafter, 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy in place; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.

Lock-in position now unanimous in round 4: 1 Jan 2022 headcount met the 25+ class for first compliance year of both duties. Disconnect duty satisfied. Electronic monitoring duty attached on 1 Jan 2022 reference date, in force 1 July 2022 for that cohort; falling to 24 mid-year does not retroactively remove duty for 2022 compliance year. Absence of any electronic monitoring policy is outstanding non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023.

Current-headcount minority view from earlier rounds – that on 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023 employer employs 24 <25 so no current electronic monitoring duty – is no longer adopted in current round.

Consensus in round 4: D is the employer not in compliance with applicable employment laws in Ontario as of 2 Jan 2023, due to missing electronic monitoring policy for a 25+ employer on the 1 Jan 2022 measuring date. Unresolved material point remains the C update timing debate, but on pleaded facts majority treats C as compliant.
